title: Timestamps that keep their nanoseconds

blocks.text: An old JDBC driver only takes and returns `java.sql.Timestamp` for a `TIMESTAMP` column, while the application works with `Instant`. Write the two conversions on `JdbcStamps`:
An instant must come back **exactly**, down to the **nanosecond**: an event at `...:00.123456789Z` must not come back as `...:00.123Z`.
The server's default time zone must make no difference: the two moments at 01:30 on 2024-11-03 in New York, when the clocks repeat an hour, stay two moments.
Columns can be empty, so **null stays null** in both directions.

cases.says: An instant with millisecond precision goes into a Timestamp and back unchanged, before and after 1970.
An instant with 123456789 nanoseconds comes back with all of them.
A null instant is written as null and a null Timestamp is read as null.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

concepts: The bridge methods Date.from and Timestamp.from throw NullPointerException for null, so nullable values are checked first.
A java.util.Date keeps only milliseconds, while Timestamp.from and toInstant keep an Instant's nanoseconds.
